purpose: Liothyronine is used to replace or supplement thyroid hormone when your thyroid gland does not make enough on its own, a condition called hypothyroidism. It may also be used to treat or prevent certain types of thyroid growths called goiters. In some cases, doctors use it as part of testing or treatment related to thyroid cancer.
how_it_works: Your thyroid gland normally makes hormones that control your body's energy and metabolism — think of it like the body's thermostat. Liothyronine is a man-made version of one of those hormones, called T3, which is the most active form. Taking this medication helps bring your hormone levels back to normal so your body can function the way it should.
common_side_effects: If your dose is too high, you may feel like your body is in overdrive — this can include a fast or pounding heartbeat, feeling hot or sweaty, shaky hands, feeling nervous or anxious, trouble sleeping, headache, or weight loss. Most side effects happen when the dose needs to be adjusted.
warnings: Do not use this medication to lose weight — it can be dangerous if your thyroid levels are already normal. Tell your doctor right away if you have chest pain, irregular heartbeat, or shortness of breath. If you have heart disease, diabetes, or adrenal problems, let your doctor know before starting this medication. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first. This medication is not safe during pregnancy unless your doctor specifically prescribes it.
typical_dosing: For most adults, the starting dose is usually 25 micrograms (mcg) taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor will check your blood levels and slowly adjust your dose every few weeks until it is just right for you. Some people take it in divided doses throughout the day. Always take it exactly as your doctor tells you to.
